analysis.one_liner: Creates a public database of clinical trial costs and requires drug makers to disclose research spending.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber; it died in the Senate Health Committee when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required drug companies to report what their clinical trials actually cost — total cost, cost per patient, and spending on personnel, supplies, and lab work — into a public, searchable federal website run by the National Institutes of Health. It also would have required publicly traded drug manufacturers to break down their research and development spending by stage in their annual filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The goal was to give the public, policymakers, and researchers hard numbers behind the prices companies charge for drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and patients, who currently see drug prices but not the research costs behind them. Policymakers debating drug pricing, and researchers studying whether drug companies' claimed research costs justify their prices, would have gained a public data source.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, taxpayers, and drug pricing researchers

how_it_helps.text: Would create a publicly searchable NIH repository where the sponsor of every applicable drug clinical trial must post total trial cost, cost per patient, and category-by-category spending on personnel, supplies, lab work, health care services, and equipment, within one year of a trial's completion.

Would require publicly traded drug manufacturers to disclose total research and development expenditures in annual SEC filings, disaggregated across basic research, pre-clinical research, and phase I, II, and III clinical trials, with signed certifications of accuracy.

The posted trial cost data would have to include the methodology behind any allocated overhead and exclude manufacturing costs of treatments the company supplied itself, aimed at preventing inflated or opaque numbers.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical and biotech companies, which would bear the cost of collecting, auditing, and reporting trial-level and stage-by-stage R&D cost data, and would lose the ability to keep that information confidential while citing high research costs to justify drug prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill only requires disclosure — it caps no prices and changes no payment rules — so any benefit to patients would arrive indirectly, through public pressure and future legislation informed by the data.

Companies would face real compliance costs to build systems that track and certify trial-level costs by category and by year, and some would argue that exposing such granular research cost data hands strategic information to competitors and could discourage investment in riskier early-stage research.

The SEC disclosure calculation excludes licensing costs, merger and acquisition costs, intangible costs tied to failure risk, and the estimated cost of capital — the very items drug companies often point to when justifying prices — which limits how complete the public picture would be.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The value depends entirely on follow-through: the bill creates public numbers but no price relief, and its exclusions would leave out some of the costs companies cite most. Still, a mandatory, certified, searchable record of what drug development actually costs is information the public does not currently have, and the compliance burden on companies is modest relative to their revenues. The stronger objection is that transparency without an enforcement mechanism may change little.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Debbie Stabenow introduced the Pharmaceutical Research Transparency Act of 2023 on May 9, 2023, with Senators Amy Klobuchar and Peter Welch as original cosponsors.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's complete action history.
The bill died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical and biotech manufacturers are better off: they never had to publish trial-level or stage-by-stage research cost data, and the pricing debate continues without those numbers. No other group gained materially.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers who avoided cost disclosure

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it for referral.

for.name: Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Peter Welch

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only the three Democratic sponsors were ever attached to the bill, and because no committee or floor vote ever happened, no record shows how the broader parties would have lined up.

industries.note: They would have had to publicly report what each clinical trial and each stage of drug R&D costs, weakening their ability to justify high prices with unverifiable research cost claims. Their interest in keeping that data confidential runs against the public's interest in seeing it.

industries.industry: Clinical research organizations and trial sponsors
industries.note: Any trial sponsor — including contract research organizations running trials for drug companies — would face new cost-tracking, certification, and one-year reporting duties on trials starting after enactment. The burden is real but narrow, and it would fall mainly on trials funded by drug makers.
